instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ. Give a short explanation referring to specific parts of the two texts.

documents.original:
Let people clip a handling note to their board when they're coming back to trim or attach a handle. A classmate can then tell whether it's okay to uncover the piece. Save some easy-reach space for anyone who would struggle to lift a loaded board above shoulder height. Date the arrival of each board so the volunteer doing the weekly round knows which owners to check in with. For a project with a separate lid, keep the two parts together on one board while they dry. The maker won't have to hunt through similar lids at the next session.

Give anyone who spots damage a way to leave the maker a private note. The owner can decide whether to repair the piece while there's still time. Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.
documents.rewrite:
Someone returning to trim a pot or add a handle could clip a note to the board saying whether a classmate may uncover it. Reserve room within easy reach for people who find it difficult to raise a full board above their shoulders. Mark each board with the date it went on the rack. On the weekly round, the volunteer can use those dates to see whose work to ask about. If a piece has a separate lid, dry both on the same board so the maker can find the right lid among the lookalikes when they come back.

Someone who notices damage should be able to get a note to the maker privately, while the maker can still choose to mend it. Members going away could name someone to look in on their work. Staff will then know whom to ask if it needs attention.

documents.original:
Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit. Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys. Publish the dimensions of a folded chair and a nested stack so a borrower can work out what will fit in their vehicle. Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery.

Allow time between bookings to check and clean a returned batch before another group expects to collect it. Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.
documents.rewrite:
An organizer looking at the shared booking calendar should be able to see how many chairs are free on the date they need and whether there's enough for their event. Ask who will have the keys and be available during the event, so a driver who's been held up knows whom to call. Give borrowers the measurements for a single folded chair and for a stack nested together. They can use those figures to plan what their vehicle will hold.

If a foot is missing or a hinge feels loose, attach an easy-to-spot repair tag and store that chair separately so it stays out of the next delivery. Space the bookings far enough apart to inspect and clean each batch after it comes back and before the next group arrives for it. A borrower should also be able to name someone else to bring the chairs back. That keeps an early departure by the organizer from holding up the return.

documents.original:
Break lines at natural points in a sentence and keep a person's first and last name together to make the text easier to take in at a glance. Start a fresh listening session with captions visible so a visitor can read the opening words without searching through settings. Ask a reviewer to follow a complete interview with the sound muted and flag places where a reply seems to come out of nowhere. Give visitors a correction slip with space for the interview title and playback time so staff can find a reported error.

Introduce a recorded letter or diary excerpt in the captions when a narrator starts reading aloud, so visitors know whose words are being quoted. For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.
documents.rewrite:
Have the captions on as soon as a new listening session begins, so visitors can catch the first words without looking for a setting. For text that's easy to read at a glance, put line breaks where the sentence naturally pauses and keep first and last names on the same line. Have someone review an interview from beginning to end with the audio off and mark any answer they couldn't see coming from what they read.

When the narrator begins to read from a letter or diary, introduce the passage in the captions and identify whose words the visitor is reading. Keep the interview title next to the captions on a looping exhibit so visitors joining halfway through know which story they've come into. For visitors who spot a mistake, provide a correction slip with room to record the title and the time in the recording. Those details will help staff locate it.

documents.original:
Give beginners a basic step they can use for a whole song, leaving them something dependable to return to when a new figure slips their mind. Make partner changes optional during the lesson so two people who feel steadier practicing together can keep their place. Teach a pair how to stop and pick up the beat again. Losing time needn't cost them the rest of the song. Put drinking water somewhere easy to spot and reach, allowing a new dancer to take a break without having to track down the host.

Walk everyone through the direction of travel on a busy floor so a new couple knows where other dancers are likely to pass. Give bags and coats a home away from the dancing area. A guest concentrating on unfamiliar steps shouldn't have to weave around belongings.
documents.rewrite:
Start beginners off with a step that will carry them through an entire song. If they forget a figure they've just learned, they have a familiar step to fall back on. During the lesson, let partners stay together if that helps them feel steady, and show them how to pause and find the beat together again so they can finish a song even after losing time.

Take everyone through the direction dancers move when the floor is busy, so a couple just starting out can anticipate where others will pass them. Find a spot off the dance floor for coats and bags so guests can concentrate on new steps with a clear path around them. Keep drinking water in plain sight and within easy reach. Newcomers can then step away for a drink without needing to find the host.

documents.original:
Save some bread from willing contributors for a later release during the advertised hours, so arriving straight from work still means finding a choice. Set out paper bags big enough for a few slices and a pencil for writing on them, so people can tell their selections apart once they're home. Ask each baker how they like to eat their bread the following day. A reheating or toasting suggestion makes a less familiar loaf easier to choose. Set a basket of spare contributions aside for people who turn up empty-handed. A batch that didn't rise shouldn't have to keep a neighbor away.

A child who wants to help could draw a little portrait of a loaf for the table, giving families something to do together without handling the samples. Invite contributors to choose a home for their spare bread in advance, allowing the closing crew to pass it along with the baker's agreement.
documents.rewrite:
Ask which contributors would be happy for some of their bread to come out later in the advertised swap hours. Holding those portions back will give neighbors coming directly from work several breads to choose from. Ask every baker for a tip on how they enjoy their loaf the next day. Knowing how the baker reheats or toasts it can help someone decide to try an unfamiliar bread. Supply paper bags that hold a few slices apiece and a pencil to label them, so people know which is which when they get home.

Keep a basket of extra contributions for anyone who arrives without bread, so a neighbor can still come if their dough failed to rise. Children keen to help could sketch a loaf for display on the table, something families can do together while leaving the samples untouched. Before closing time, invite each contributor to choose where any bread they have left should go. The closing crew can then pass it on knowing the baker agrees.

documents.original:
Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier. A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page. Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look. Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

Give finished volumes a shelf sorted by season, so a returning visitor can find what other people noticed during the same month in earlier years. Offer an occasional quiet drawing period before a garden tour, letting visitors who like to observe in silence try the books in company.
documents.rewrite:
Invite a gardener to leave a pencil sketch in progress on one of the first pages. Seeing a few tentative strokes can make it easier to risk an imperfect line in a book everyone can see. Put scraps of paper in the pencil tray, too, so visitors can try out a mark in private before drawing it in the book. Someone unsure how to fit a whole border onto a page could use a small cardboard viewfinder to frame just a few stems.

Beside each drawing, leave room to say where in the garden the plant grows. A visitor taken with a sketch of a seed head can then find it and have a closer look. Arrange the filled books by season on a shelf so people coming back can look up what caught other visitors' eyes that month in years past. An occasional spell of quiet drawing before a garden tour would give people who enjoy observing in silence a chance to try the sketchbooks alongside others.

documents.original:
Send each performer a short list of what to wear or bring, since a trouser hem measured over slippers may sit differently over the show shoes. Allow a little extra time for people with several changes, so one elaborate costume doesn't quietly push the rest of the evening behind. Let performers send word to one named contact if their journey is delayed, so the team can fill a gap while there's still time to use it. Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer.

Have the note taker read back the requested change while the costume is still on, when a misunderstood sleeve length takes seconds to put right. Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.
documents.rewrite:
Before the fitting, give each performer a brief list of things to bring or wear. The length that looks right when you pin trousers over slippers can change once the performer puts on their show shoes. Book a little longer for performers who need to change several times, so a single complicated costume doesn't delay everyone after them. Give performers one person's name for reporting travel delays. With early word, the team can still make use of an opening in the schedule.

Put a legible clock where the fitter can see it and keep track of the appointment while keeping their attention on the performer. Before the performer takes the costume off, ask the person taking notes to read the alteration back. If they understood the sleeve length differently, there's still time to settle it in seconds. When the sewing exceeds what the team can finish, record which jobs everyone agreed should come first so a costume due at rehearsal tomorrow gets worked on in time.

documents.original:
Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match. Offer a small sign that a seated player can turn toward the door when they'd welcome an opponent, taking the guesswork out of joining a stranger. Keep a written waiting list during busy periods, letting visitors sit down to read instead of hovering over games that look nearly finished. Invite both players to agree before starting whether they'll allow takebacks, heading off a dispute the first time someone overlooks a check.

Set up a place for post-game discussion a little away from the quiet boards, since a lively analysis can last much longer than the game itself. Encourage a quiet word with the host if a disagreement develops, giving players a way to settle a rules question without drawing in the whole room.
documents.rewrite:
Give a helper a demonstration board in a corner clear of the games in progress. They can show a position there without drawing onlookers around another player's match. A seated player who's ready for company could turn a small sign toward the door, so a newcomer knows they're welcome to join. When the room fills up, keep a written waiting list so visitors can sit and read while they wait for a board to open up, even if a game nearby looks nearly over.

Before the first move, encourage the two players to settle whether moves can be taken back. They'll already have an agreement to go by if one of them misses a check. Set aside space a short distance from the quiet boards to talk through a finished game, since an animated discussion can go on well beyond the time it took to play. If a disagreement arises, suggest speaking quietly to the host so players can resolve a question about the rules without involving everybody else.
